en: The Theravāda Vinaya:
The Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga,
Chapter on Saṅghādisesa Offenses.
11. The Training Rule on Being Angry over a Legal Issue At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the bhikkhunī Caṇḍakāḷī, having been rebuked in some legal issue, being angry and displeased, spoke thus:
“There are bhikkhunīs who act out of desire, bhikkhunīs who act out of hatred, bhikkhunīs who act out of delusion, and bhikkhunīs who act out of fear.
Those bhikkhunīs who were of few desires … [as before] … complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
“How can the noble lady Caṇḍakāḷī, when she has been dealt with regarding some legal issue and is angry and displeased, speak thus?”
“Bhikkhunīs who follow their own desires... bhikkhunīs who follow out of fear.
... “Is it true, bhikkhus, that the bhikkhunī Caṇḍakāḷī, having been rebuked in some legal matter, being angry and displeased, says this:
‘Bhikkhunīs who follow their own desires... bhikkhunīs who follow out of fear’?”
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“… How, monks, can the bhikkhunī Caṇḍakāḷī, when she has been dealt with in some legal matter and is angry and displeased, speak thus?”
“Monks, there are nuns who act out of desire... and there are nuns who act out of fear.
Monks, this does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
And thus, monks, let the nuns recite this training rule:
“Whatever nun, being rebuked in some legal matter, being angry and displeased, should speak thus:
‘The nuns act out of favoritism; the nuns act out of ill will; the nuns act out of delusion;
the nuns act out of fear,’ that nun should be addressed by the nuns thus:”
"Venerable lady, when you were accused in some legal matter and were angry, displeased, and resentful, you spoke thus:
'The nuns are swayed by favoritism, the nuns are swayed by ill will, the nuns are swayed by delusion, and the nuns are swayed by fear.
Yet, venerable lady, you might indeed act out of favoritism, you might act out of ill will, you might act out of delusion, and you might act out of fear."

And if that bhikkhunī, being thus addressed by the bhikkhunīs, should persist as before, that bhikkhunī is to be formally admonished by the bhikkhunīs up to three times for the sake of relinquishing that [behavior].
If, being admonished up to three times, she relinquishes it, that is good;

if she does not relinquish it, this bhikkhunī also has committed an offense that is an offense entailing a formal meeting of the Saṅgha (saṅghādisesa), which involves a process of reconciliation after the third admonition.
"But whichever" means whichever such... "nun" means...
[as before]... nun.
…pe… this is the nun intended in this context.
"In regard to some legal issue" (*kismiñcideva adhikaraṇe*):

a legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) consists of four types of legal issues—the legal issue of dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*), the legal issue of accusation (*anuvādādhikaraṇa*), the legal issue of offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*), and the legal issue of business (*kiccādhikaraṇa*).
"Overcome" means she is said to be defeated.
"Angry and displeased" means—
“Displeased, with hearts struck down, and harboring resentment, she might speak thus:
‘The bhikkhunīs act out of favoritism... [and so on] ...the bhikkhunīs act out of fear.’”
"That bhikkhunī" refers to whichever bhikkhunī speaks in such a manner.
"By the bhikkhunīs" refers to...
By other bhikkhunīs. Those who see it or hear of it should say to her:
"Venerable lady, do not speak thus in regard to some legal issue, being resentful, angry, and displeased:
'The bhikkhunīs act out of favoritism... [and so on] ...the bhikkhunīs act out of fear.'"
“Venerable Chandā might indeed go out of favoritism … or she might go out of fear.
This should be said a second time;
it should be said a third time.
If he relinquishes it, that is good;
if he does not relinquish it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If they hear [the accusation] and do not speak, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
That nun, even if she has been dragged into the midst of the Saṅgha, should be told:
"Venerable lady, do not speak thus in regard to any legal matter while being accused, angry, and displeased:
'The nuns act out of favoritism... [and so on] ...the nuns act out of fear.'"
“Venerable Chandā might indeed go out of favoritism … or she might go out of fear.
This should be said a second time;
it should be said a third time.
If she relinquishes it, that is well;
if she does not relinquish it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
That bhikkhunī is to be formally admonished.
“And furthermore, monks, they should be admonished thus:
An experienced and competent nun should inform the Saṅgha:
‘Let the noble Saṅgha listen to me. This nun, so-and-so, having been rebuked in some disciplinary matter, being angry and displeased, speaks thus:’”
“The bhikkhunīs act out of desire... [as before] ...and the bhikkhunīs act out of fear.
She does not relinquish that matter.
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha should formally admonish the bhikkhunī named so-and-so for the relinquishing of that matter.
This is the motion.
Let the noble Saṅgha hear me:
this bhikkhunī, so-and-so, having been rebuked in some legal matter, being angry and displeased, speaks thus—
“The nuns are prone to favoritism … [and so on] … the nuns are prone to fear.
She does not relinquish that matter.
The Saṅgha formally admonishes the nun named so-and-so for the relinquishing of that matter.
Whichever noble lady approves of the formal admonition of the bhikkhunī named so-and-so for the sake of her relinquishing that matter, let her be silent;
whichever does not approve, let her speak. A second time I speak this matter... [as before] ...pe... [as before] ...pe... [as before] ...pe... [as before].
For a third time I speak this matter...
[as before] ...The Saṅgha has formally admonished the bhikkhunī so-and-so for the relinquishing of that matter.
It is pleasing to the Saṅgha; therefore, by silence, I hold it thus."
For the motion, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
For two proclamations, there are offenses of serious transgression (thullaccaya).
At the conclusion of the proclamation, there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
For one who commits a *saṅghādisesa* offense, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) at the motion (*ñatti*).
With two proclamations (*kammavācā*), the grave offenses (*thullaccaya*) are extinguished.
This too—
It is said with reference to the preceding [offenses].
"Up to the third time" means that one incurs [the offense] through being exhorted up to the third time, not simultaneously with the transgression of the matter itself.
"Leading to expulsion" means one is expelled from the Saṅgha.
"Saṅghādisesa" [means...]
...pe... for that reason also it is called a *saṅghādisesa*.
If, regarding a legitimate legal act (*dhammakamma*), one perceives it as a legitimate legal act and does not desist, there is an offense of *saṅghādisesa*.
If, regarding a legitimate legal act, one is uncertain and does not desist, there is an offense of *saṅghādisesa*.
If it is an illegal act, but one perceives it as a legal act and does not relinquish it, there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
If it is an illegal act, but one perceives it as a legal act, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If it is an illegal act, but one is uncertain of it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is an illegitimate legal procedure and one perceives it as such, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
There is no offense for one who does not formally admonish [the offender].
For one who relinquishes it,
for one who is insane,
and for one who is a first-offender.
The eighth Saṅghādisesa training rule is concluded.
